opus-5.5.text:
I think evolution is part of the story, but I'm not sure it explains as much as people sometimes assume. There's a real distinction to draw here.

For some things, evolution clearly gave us a lot. Vision, hearing, locomotion: our ancestors needed these for hundreds of millions of years, so it's very plausible we have strong priors built in. A child learns to walk or recognize objects quickly, and you can say, well, evolution did most of the work. A squirrel can do a lot of this too.

But then look at language, math, coding. These are extremely recent, far too recent for evolution to have specifically prepared us for them. And yet people learn them with remarkable sample efficiency. Someone can become a decent programmer in a few months, from a tiny amount of data compared with what a model sees. And they generalize better. They're more robust. They don't make the strange mistakes models make, where something works beautifully in one setting and falls apart in a slightly different one.

So to me that suggests there's something about human learning itself that is just better. It's not only a strong prior about the world. It's that the learning machinery is fundamentally more efficient and more general.

One clue might be something like a value function, an internal sense of whether things are going well or badly, before you get any external reward. A teenager learning to drive has that. They feel when they're doing poorly and correct themselves after maybe ten hours of practice. Emotions might play that role in humans in a surprisingly robust way. That kind of self-correcting, continual learning is something our current methods don't really have.

So my answer is that evolution explains some of it, especially for ancient skills. But for the newer skills, I think there's a principle of learning we haven't found yet. I have opinions about what it might be, but unfortunately I can't discuss all of them in detail.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution supplied strong built-in priors for ancient skills such as vision, which is a small amount of highly useful information for learning.

r002.rationale: It says children learn to recognize objects quickly, but does not mention that this happens despite limited diversity in their early visual experience.

r003.rationale: It argues that humans learn language, math, and coding efficiently despite these being too recent for evolution to have specifically prepared us, and says humans generalize better than models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot, and I think it's genuinely one of the most important open questions. So let me try to say what I think is true and what I think is not.

The naive version of the evolution argument is: humans learn from very little data because evolution did a huge amount of pretraining for us. Billions of years of search over genomes, and the result is that we're born with a lot of built-in structure, and so the "sample efficiency" you see in a human lifetime is kind of an illusion. The real training set is the whole history of life.

I think there's something to that, but I don't think it's the whole explanation, and I actually think it's mostly not the explanation. Here's why. If you look at how much information the genome can actually transmit, it's small. It's on the order of a gigabyte or less, and most of that isn't about the brain. So whatever evolution gave us, it has to be compact. It can't be a huge pretrained model in the sense of a lot of specific knowledge. It has to be more like a prior, or a learning algorithm, or an architecture, something that's quite small in bits but very powerful in effect.

And actually there's some evidence for this if you look across species. A horse can walk within an hour of being born. That looks very much like evolution did the work directly. But humans aren't like that. Humans come out very incompetent, and then they learn a huge amount. And the stuff that humans are best at, language, abstract reasoning, mathematics, driving a car, these are things evolution had very little or no time to directly optimize for. So you can't say evolution installed the skills. What it must have done is install a very good learner.

So then the real question becomes: what does that learner have that our models don't? And I honestly don't fully know. But I'd point to a couple of things. One is that a human doesn't learn from "little data" in the way we usually mean it. A child gets years of continuous, embodied, multimodal experience, and crucially they get to act in the world and see what happens. That's a very different kind of data than static text. A second thing is that whatever the human learning algorithm is, it seems to generalize from very few examples in a way that's robust. A teenager with ten hours of driving is a reasonable driver. We don't have that. Our models need enormous amounts of data and still generalize worse.

So my view is: evolution matters, but it matters as the thing that found the right prior and the right learning algorithm, not as a replacement for learning. And the fact that it managed to do that in such a small number of bits is actually encouraging. It means the thing we're missing is probably not some giant amount of knowledge. It's probably some relatively compact principle that we haven't figured out yet. And I think that's the most interesting research question there is right now.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution supplied a compact prior or learning algorithm that is powerful in effect, rather than a large amount of specific knowledge.

r002.rationale: It discusses children's embodied experience but does not mention strong visual recognition or limited diversity in their early visual experience.

r003.rationale: It says humans learn skills such as driving and abstract reasoning that evolution had little time to optimize for, and contrasts human generalization from few examples with AI models’ data needs.

astra-6.text:
I think evolution is part of the explanation, but the question is what, exactly, it explains. Evolution has had an enormous amount of experience, and some of that experience is encoded in our brains. So when we say a human learns from very little data, we’re not counting whatever evolution has already supplied.

But I don’t think that settles the question. Humans can learn things like mathematics or programming, which didn’t exist in the evolutionary environment. It’s hard to argue that evolution directly gave us knowledge of those things. It seems to have given us a learning procedure that can be applied to situations very different from the ones that produced it.

So then the question becomes: what is that learning procedure? What structure does it have that allows it to use experience so efficiently? Saying “evolution” gives you an explanation for where it came from, but it doesn’t yet tell you how it works. And that’s the part we’d like to understand.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution supplied an enormous amount of experience, but does not characterize it as a small amount of exceptionally useful information.

r002.rationale: The response does not discuss children’s visual recognition or the limited diversity of their early visual experience.

r003.rationale: The response names mathematics and programming as abilities outside the evolutionary environment, but does not say humans retain a sample-efficiency advantage over AI models in those abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evolution is part of the explanation, but we have to be careful about what we mean by learning from little data. By the time a human learns a new concept from one example, they’ve already had years of experience with the world. So it’s one example on top of a very large amount of prior learning.

Then there’s the question of what evolution contributes. It clearly gives us something: the architecture of the brain, the learning rules, motivations, perhaps predispositions that make certain things easier to learn. But that’s different from saying that evolution has somehow put all our knowledge into the brain.

The interesting question is how much of human learning efficiency comes from those evolved ingredients, and how much comes from having a better learning algorithm. I don’t think we know how to separate those cleanly. Evolution is an explanation for where the system came from, but by itself it doesn’t tell us which properties of the system make learning so efficient.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution supplies brain architecture, learning rules, motivations, and predispositions, but does not characterize this as a small amount of exceptionally useful information.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss children’s visual recognition or the limited diversity of their early visual experience.

r003.rationale: It raises uncertainty about evolved ingredients versus learning algorithms, but does not claim humans retain an advantage in abilities evolution is unlikely to explain.
